explanations: terra: Adam and his spouse are told to dwell in the Garden and eat freely from it, joining settled household companionship to abundant accessible food.

terra: Israel asks to exchange one food for a list of ordinary crops, and misery is then laid upon them; food and the س ك ن family's maskanah branch meet here in a different sense from settled household shelter.
terra: The covenant places good treatment of orphans and the needy beside kind speech, prayer, and almsgiving, the same union of worship and household-facing care.

luna: The source section’s ط ع م root names food and feeding and its scene names the orphan and poor; 2:177 describes giving wealth, despite love for it, to relatives, orphans, the needy, travelers, and askers, showing what the withheld provision could become. | terra: Righteousness includes giving loved wealth to relatives, orphans, the needy, travelers, and askers alongside prayer; belief is tested through the same household-facing recipients.

luna: This ayah allows a feeding ransom for a poor person in the context of fasting; it is a concrete measured food provision for a miskin, matching the section’s link between food and the person left without it. | terra: Feeding a needy person is the compensating duty for one unable to fast, so food placed within reach becomes a concrete act of worship.

luna: The section makes household food and small supplies the means of care for the vulnerable; 2:215 answers what to spend by naming parents, relatives, orphans, the needy, and travelers, specifying recipients for such provision. | terra: Asked what to spend, the answer directs good wealth to parents, relatives, orphans, the needy, and the traveler, locating giving in the household's nearest circles and beyond.
terra: When asked what to spend, the answer is the surplus, a precise bridge to lending or giving what the house can release without ceasing to stand.

luna: The section describes the orphan as a fatherless child treated as an outsider and pushed away; 2:220 says that improving the orphans’ affairs is best and that mixing with them makes them brothers, directly answering the image’s exclusion from the household. | terra: Improving the affairs of orphans is best, and mixing life with them makes them brothers; this replaces the expelled child with an orphan incorporated into the household.

luna: The section defines the orphan as a child whose father has died and places household food under that child’s care; 2:233 assigns the nursing mother’s food and clothing to the father, showing the household support whose loss makes the orphan vulnerable. | terra: A father owes nursing mothers food and clothing according to what is fair, and neither parent is to be harmed through the child; household sustenance is measured around a small dependent.
terra: A divorced woman is to receive a gift according to the giver's means and recognized good, a measured household transfer that preserves care at separation.
terra: A widow is assigned maintenance for a year without expulsion from the house, joining continued provision to continued shelter when her household guardian is lost.
terra: Divorced women are owed a provision according to recognized good, another household boundary where useful goods must leave the holder's hand as a due.
terra: The good loan to God is multiplied on return, a theological analogue to the section's loaned household object that leaves the hand yet is not finally lost.

luna: The section describes grain settling in a shaken measure until more fits and the bowl fills; 2:261 also uses grain growing into abundant provision, though its point is the multiplied reward of spending rather than filling a household vessel. | terra: Spending is likened to a grain producing many ears, transforming the section's individual grains in a filled measure into an image of provision multiplied by release.
terra: A kind word and forgiveness are better than charity followed by injury; like 4:8, it keeps material provision and maʿrūf speech under one ethic.
terra: Charity is voided by reminders, injury, and spending to be seen by people; provision leaving the hand must differ inwardly from the surah's display-oriented worship.
terra: The parable asks the reader to imagine a garden destroyed when its owner has weak young children, making the fragility of dependents and the loss of household sustenance emotionally concrete.

luna: The section’s al-maʿūn list names useful everyday household things; 2:267 warns against selecting for charity what the giver would accept only with eyes closed, a specific standard for the quality of goods shared. | terra: Give from the good things acquired and do not select defective goods one would accept only reluctantly, applying a quality test to what comes off the household shelf.
terra: Concealed charity delivered to the poor is called better for the giver, providing the positive counterpart to public display while keeping the needy recipient in view.
terra: The poor restrained in God's cause do not ask importunately and may be mistaken for self-sufficient; the household must notice need beyond the neighbor who knocks.
terra: A debtor in hardship must receive time, and remitting the debt is better; this sets compassion above the lender's expectation of return when the borrower truly cannot restore what was lent.
terra: Whenever Zechariah enters Mary's sanctuary he finds provision with her, and she says it is from God; guardianship, an interior place, and unexpected food meet in one scene.

terra: Some entrusted with a great sum return it, while another will not return even a single coin unless persistently pressed; the ayah tests the section's expectation that a borrowed household item normally comes back.

luna: The section contrasts keeping food and household goods with giving them; 3:92 says righteousness is not attained until one gives from what one loves, a specific bridge to the loved food in 76:8 and the small things held back here. | terra: Righteousness is not reached until people spend from what they love, reversing the instinct to lend only what is negligible or fill another's dish only after keeping the desired food.
terra: Maskanah is laid upon the condemned people, using the section's س ك ن family for abjection rather than dwelling or household provision and thus marking a secondary semantic boundary.
terra: The righteous spend in both ease and hardship, refusing to turn a less-than-full household into a blanket excuse for withholding.

luna: The section shows household goods held back from the needy; 3:180 rejects the idea that withholding what God has given is good and pictures that hoarded bounty as a collar on the Day of Resurrection. | terra: Those who are stingy with what God gave them mistake withholding for good, directly challenging the belief that retained stores secure the house.

luna: The section depicts the fatherless child kept from household provision; 4:2 commands guardians to give orphans their property and not consume it with their own, extending care from food and small goods to the child’s estate. | terra: Give orphans their property and do not consume it into your own; the guardian's stocked house must release what belongs to the child.

terra: Fear of failing to deal justly with orphan girls governs whether their guardians may marry them, exposing how entry into the guardian's own household can either protect or exploit the fatherless.
terra: Guardians must provide food and clothing from the property they manage and speak kindly, joining sustaining goods with the respectful welcome also required in 4:8.

luna: The section defines the orphan as fatherless until maturity; 4:6 describes testing orphans until they reach marriageable age and then handing over their property if sound, giving a practical household-care boundary to that definition. | terra: Test orphans until marriageable age and then deliver their property without wasteful or hasty consumption; it supplies the maturity boundary in the section's definition of yatīm.

luna: The section connects household stores and the small kindness of al-maʿūn with recognized good; 4:8 says that when relatives, orphans, and the poor attend an inheritance division, they should receive a share and kind words, making provision in the household setting concrete. | terra: At inheritance division, relatives, orphans, and the needy who are present must receive provision and a kind word; the household door remains open when goods are apportioned.

luna: The section defines the orphan as a child left fatherless and makes the home’s provisions part of that child’s vulnerability; 4:9 asks people handling inheritance to imagine leaving weak offspring behind and fear for them, between 4:8’s instruction to give and 4:10’s warning against consuming orphan property. | terra: Those who fear leaving vulnerable young children behind must fear God and speak rightly, asking the householder to see an orphan through the vulnerability of his own small dependents.

luna: The section’s orphan is denied what a household should offer; 4:10 names consuming orphans’ property unjustly as swallowing fire, a sharp reversal of the care and provision the child lacks. | terra: Consuming orphan property is described as swallowing fire, exposing the violence hidden when a guardian fills his own vessels from a fatherless child's goods.
terra: Household maintainers are identified partly by spending from their wealth, making provision for those within the home a constitutive responsibility rather than an optional favor.

luna: The section imagines a neighbor coming to the door for food or a useful household object; 4:36 specifically commands good treatment of the near and distant neighbor, alongside the orphan, needy, and traveler, locating the small domestic kindness within neighborly duty. | terra: The command to do good names orphans, the needy, the near neighbor, the distant neighbor, and the traveler; it supplies the full social map of the person arriving at a household door.

luna: The section cites م ن ع and glosses its miserly form as a person who is stingy and holds back; 4:37 depicts those who are stingy, urge stinginess, and conceal God’s bounty, closely matching the named disposition and hidden stores. | terra: The condemned are stingy, command others to stinginess, and conceal what God gave them, echoing the person who neither feeds nor urges feeding.
terra: Those who spend their wealth to be seen by people are condemned, clarifying that a visible gift can reproduce the same display that empties prayer of care.
terra: God does not wrong even an atom's weight and multiplies a good deed; the section's tiny, easy kindness is therefore small in cost but not in moral weight.
terra: If such people possessed a share of dominion, they would not give others even a naqīr, the speck on a date stone; this is the section's refusal of the tiny, easy thing in Quranic scale.

luna: This ayah addresses orphan girls whose guardians withhold what is due to them and commands justice toward vulnerable children; it extends the section’s fatherless-child scene from food and shelter to the guardian’s duty not to deny her rights. | terra: The ruling demands justice for orphan women denied what is assigned to them and for vulnerable children, extending the section's small fatherless child to household guardianship and property.
terra: The covenant combines establishing prayer, giving alms, and lending God a good loan, directly uniting worship with releasing goods under a promise of return.

luna: In the oath-expiration rule, this ayah requires feeding ten poor people from the average food one gives one’s own household. That is a concrete household-to-poor transfer matching the section’s filled bowl and food for the miskin. | terra: The expiation feeds ten needy people from the average food one feeds one's own family, explicitly measuring the visitor's dish by the household table.

luna: For a hunting violation during pilgrimage, this ayah allows an expiation by feeding needy people; the specific food-for-needy provision offers another concrete instance of the transfer the section’s withholding scene suppresses. | terra: One form of hunting expiation is food for needy people, another concrete setting in which edible household value is transferred to the poor.

luna: The disciples ask Jesus for a table spread with food from heaven; the section names the sofra cloth among ordinary household goods and develops food placed in a filled bowl, so this is a direct table-and-meal scene. | terra: The disciples ask whether a table spread can be sent from heaven, turning the request for food and a provisioned table into an explicit address to the giver.

luna: This ayah says the disciples want to eat from the table and have their hearts reassured; it completes the request in 5:112 by stating the meal’s role for those who will share it. | terra: They say they wish to eat from the table and have their hearts reassured, naming actual eating rather than possession of unused provision.

luna: Jesus asks for a table to be sent down as a feast for the first and last of them; this ayah supplies the communal meal requested in 5:112 and connects a shared table with provision. | terra: Jesus asks for a table from heaven as a recurring feast and calls God the best provider, contrasting divine provision with the human appeal to God as a reason not to feed.

luna: God answers that the table will be sent down and sets a severe boundary for anyone who disbelieves afterward; it completes 5:112–114’s scene of provision with the consequence attached to receiving it. | terra: God answers that He will send the table down, completing the request-and-gift movement that the withholding household interrupts.
terra: God is described as feeding while not needing to be fed; this separates the divine provider from the dependent human householder who cites God's will to avoid sharing provision.
terra: Night is made سَكَنًا, using the source section's dwelling root for repose rather than a house; it weakly clarifies the rest and stability underlying the household sense.

luna: The section links grain, a filled measure, and food for the needy; 6:141 speaks of eating the crop when it bears fruit and giving its due on harvest day, connecting provision directly to distribution. | terra: The command to eat from the harvest and give its due on harvest day puts the grain, the household's consumption, and the recipient's share together before storage can become withholding.
terra: Do not kill children because of poverty, for God provides for parent and child; fear of an empty pantry cannot erase the dependent child's claim.

luna: The section joins the orphan to the filling and measuring of household food; 6:152 puts both concerns in one command, protecting an orphan’s property until maturity and requiring full measure and just weight, so a child’s due and a measured allotment meet in the same ayah. | terra: One ayah joins the section's two central charges: protect the orphan's property until maturity and give full measure and weight; the guarded child and the honestly filled vessel belong to one justice.
terra: The repeated command has Adam and his spouse dwell in the Garden and eat wherever they wish, another direct coupling of س ك ن dwelling and provision.

terra: The people of the Fire ask for water or some of God's provision and are refused because those gifts are forbidden to them, an eschatological boundary where refusal is judgment rather than household miserliness.
terra: Shuayb commands full measure and weight and forbids diminishing people's goods, making honest provision part of social repair.
terra: The spouse is made so the human being may dwell in tranquility with her, another household sense of the section's س ك ن root beyond a building or stored ration.

luna: The ayah allocates a share of war gains to orphans, the needy, and the traveler; it gives a concrete instance of household-like resources being directed to the very vulnerable recipients whom the section’s man leaves without support. | terra: A stated share of spoils belongs to relatives, orphans, the needy, and travelers, making provision for the fatherless and poor a claim on newly acquired goods.
terra: Those who hoard gold and silver and do not spend it in God's way are warned, turning retained household wealth into an explicit instance of stored usefulness denied circulation.
terra: The hoarded metal is heated and used to brand its owners, so the substance kept back becomes the instrument that exposes and punishes withholding.
terra: The hypocrites are told that spending willingly or unwillingly will not be accepted, establishing the inward boundary for the reluctant expenditure diagnosed with lazy prayer in 9:54.

terra: The ayah uses the withholding root for what prevents hypocrites' expenditures from acceptance, then says they approach prayer lazily and spend reluctantly; worship and the closed hand expose one another.
terra: Obligatory alms are assigned to the poor and needy among named recipients, placing stored wealth under claims outside its owner's household.
terra: The hypocrites close their hands, a bodily picture of the same hand that refuses the small object or food despite having it within reach.
terra: People promise that if God gives them bounty they will give charity and be righteous; 9:76 shows the stocked hand breaking precisely this promise.

luna: The source section’s dictionary gloss for م ن ع describes the miserly person as holding back; 9:76 shows people who, after receiving bounty, become stingy with it and turn away, making the withholding an action rather than only a label. | terra: After God grants bounty, they become stingy and turn away, showing how a filled store can harden into the very withholding the gift should have ended.
terra: Those who mock believers able to give only their effort are condemned, protecting the moral value of a genuinely small contribution from contempt.
terra: No expenditure, small or large, goes unrecorded, explicitly protecting the moral significance of the section's slight and easy contribution.
terra: Night is made for people to rest in, repeating the section's س ك ن root-family idea of repose without itself depicting a house or material provision.
terra: God guarantees every creature's provision and knows its settled place and repository, placing sustenance, dwelling, and storage within one divine account.
terra: Abraham promptly brings a roasted calf to visiting messengers; the home answers arrival with prepared food, the direct opposite of the town that refuses two hungry travelers.
terra: Shuayb forbids deficient measure and weight while acknowledging his people's prosperity, exposing abundance as no excuse for giving others less.
terra: He commands full measure and weight in justice and forbids diminishing people's things, joining the well-filled container to respect for others' goods.

terra: After Shuayb commands full measure, his people ask whether his prayer orders them to abandon doing whatever they wish with their wealth; the passage explicitly makes prayer accountable for economic conduct.
terra: A water drawer lowers his bucket and brings the separated boy Joseph up from the well; the source dictionary's loanable bucket becomes an implement that reaches a vulnerable child.

terra: The separated boy Joseph is sold for a few coins and treated as of little value, showing the cruel reversal in which the vulnerable child, rather than a utensil, becomes the cheap disposable thing.
terra: The Egyptian buyer tells his wife to honor the boy's lodging and considers adopting him, reversing expulsion by receiving a separated child into the home.

luna: The section’s cited household-benefit list includes a knife among ordinary items that may be borrowed; 12:31 places knives in the women’s hands during a gathering at the house, a specific domestic-use scene for one of those small tools. | terra: Each guest is given a knife before the women cut their hands; the dictionary's ordinary lendable knife appears as shared table equipment, while the injury marks a real boundary to the claim that such tools are harmless to pass.
terra: Joseph orders seven years of cultivation and tells the people to leave grain in its ears except the little they eat, giving a concrete scene of food retained for future household survival.
terra: Seven hard years will consume what was stored except a little kept in reserve, marking necessary preservation as a boundary distinct from miserly withholding.
terra: Joseph fully equips his brothers with their provisions before setting the condition about their brother, establishing the granary as a place able to fill a family's containers.
terra: No measure will be given if the brother is not brought, setting the explicit boundary whose later report is مَنَعَ مِنَّا ٱلْكَيْلُ in 12:63.
terra: Joseph has their merchandise returned inside their saddlebags, a material enactment of the section's point that what leaves a generous store may come back.

luna: The section names م ن ع as the root of withholding and cites the filled measure; in 12:63 the brothers say مُنِعَ مِنَّا الْكَيْلُ, that the ration is withheld from them. In its context they need another family provision from Egypt and ask to take Benjamin so they can measure grain again, tying refusal to household food. | terra: مُنِعَ مِنَّا ٱلْكَيْلُ puts the section's withholding root directly upon a grain measure, fusing its withheld utensil and shaken-full measure in one clause.

luna: The brothers find their traded goods returned in their baggage and say they can now obtain provisions for their family. This is not a borrowed pot, but it is a specific, indirect parallel to the section’s claim that small goods given from a household often return while the household gets what it needs. | terra: The brothers discover their goods returned and expect another camel-load, calling it an easy measure; returned goods, added provision, and ease converge on the section's household image.

luna: The section names pots and useful household objects, and also develops grain being shaken into a measure; 12:70 places Joseph’s cup in a brother’s bag after provisioning the family, joining a concrete vessel to a ration scene, though here it serves a plot rather than a loan. | terra: Joseph places the drinking cup in his brother's bag; a portable household vessel enters the same grain-measure story that the section connects to withheld measure.

luna: After the provisions and hidden cup of 12:70, the brothers turn back and ask what is missing; 12:72 names the king’s cup. The section’s inventory of loanable household objects has a concrete, though royal and accusatory, counterpart in this missing vessel.

luna: This ayah identifies the missing object in the scene begun at 12:70 as the king’s measuring cup and offers a camel-load to its finder; it links a household vessel with measured food provision, while its royal setting differs from the neighbor’s small loan. | terra: The missing royal cup is paired with a camel-load reward and functions within the provision scene, showing one vessel at the junction of drinking ware and measured grain.
terra: A family struck by hardship arrives with scant merchandise and asks Joseph to give full measure and be charitable, putting need, request, giver, and brimming measure into one scene.

terra: Abraham says he has settled descendants in a barren valley by the Sacred House so that they establish prayer, then asks that they receive fruit; household, children, prayer, and provision meet in one appeal.
terra: God holds the treasuries of all things and sends each down only in known measure, scaling the stocked shelf and measured container into a governed economy of provision.

luna: The section depicts a householder withholding small material benefits; 16:71 asks why those favored in provision would not share their provision with those under their authority, making withheld household resources a concrete analogy in its argument against denying God’s favor.

luna: The section cites the س ك ن root for a home, its people, and what lets people dwell there; 16:80 says God made homes سَكَنًا, a place of settlement, giving the domestic word behind the poor person’s name a concrete Quranic home scene. | terra: God makes houses a سَكَنًا, using the source section's س ك ن root in its concrete household sense: a dwelling is meant to provide settled shelter.

terra: A secure town receiving abundant provision from every direction denies God's favors and is made to taste hunger and fear; plentiful stores become a test whose failure ends in the lack imposed on others.

luna: The section imagines a small household benefit being asked for by someone nearby; 17:26 orders giving relatives, the needy, and the traveler their due, translating the stored household resource into a duty to provide. | terra: Give the relative, the needy, and the traveler their due; the recipient's share is named as a right, not an optional small favor.

luna: The section’s needy person comes to ask at the door and receives no encouragement; 17:28 addresses turning away from needy relatives, poor, or travelers when one lacks means and commands a gracious word, preserving kindness even when one cannot give.

luna: The section names withholding through root م ن ع and describes a hand that grips small useful things; 17:29 pictures the hand tied to the neck as stinginess and sets it against reckless spending, making the closed hand visible. | terra: Do not keep the hand chained to the neck or extend it without limit; this gives the image's withholding hand a boundary of responsible household spending.
terra: Do not kill children for fear of poverty, for God provides for them and their parents; anticipated scarcity is rejected as a reason to close provision against small dependents.

luna: The section’s named orphan is a child whose household provision is vulnerable; 17:34 sets a boundary around approaching an orphan’s property except in the best manner until maturity, completing the neighboring measure command in 17:35 with a rule against taking from the child. | terra: It forbids approaching the orphan's property except beneficially until maturity; 17:35 then moves directly to the full measure, reproducing the section's meeting of orphan-care and a filled measure.

luna: The section’s cited dictionary form دعدع مكيالا describes shaking a measure until it is full; 17:35 commands full measure and fair weighing, completing 17:34’s protection of the orphan’s property with fair dealing in provisions. | terra: The command to give full measure and weigh justly completes 17:34's rule for orphan property, setting honest filling beside care for the fatherless exactly as the section does.

terra: Even if people owned the treasuries of divine mercy, they would hold back from fear of depletion; it states the false scarcity behind refusing an item that returns and scarcely diminishes the house.
terra: The sleepers send one companion with silver to find wholesome food and bring provision back, a compact household-like scene of entrusted money, procurement, and shared food.
terra: The record omits neither a small thing nor a great one, a general but specific answer to the belief that refusal of a trivial household aid is beneath account.

luna: The section’s named طَعَام and root ط ع م link food to feeding; here Moses and his companion ask the town’s people for food, and they refuse to host them (فَأَبَوْا أَن يُضَيِّفُوهُمَا), a concrete scene of denied hospitality. | terra: موسى and his companion ask a town's people for food, but the people refuse hospitality; this stages the petitioner, stocked household, and withholding hand at an actual door.

terra: The servant explains that he damaged a boat belonging to needy workers to save it from seizure; in the same interpretive sequence as 18:82, a poor household's useful asset is secretly preserved.

luna: The section describes the orphan inside a household from which care and provision are withheld; 18:82 reveals that the wall and hidden treasure belong to two orphan boys and are preserved for them because their father was righteous, a specific case of safeguarding an orphan household’s future. | terra: The repaired wall belongs to two orphan boys and hides their treasure until they mature; divine guardianship preserves a fatherless household's provision in the town that denied food.
terra: Ishmael commands his household to prayer and almsgiving, the positive household counterpart to prayer that leaves food and useful goods withheld.
terra: Command your household to pray and persist, while God says He asks no provision and provides for them; family prayer and household sustenance are held together rather than split apart.
terra: Even a deed the weight of a mustard seed is brought into the just balance, giving the section's tiny, easy kindness a precise moral weight.
terra: Sacrificial livestock are to be eaten from and used to feed the afflicted poor, turning a household's meat into a shared meal rather than stored abundance.
terra: After mentioning eating, the ayah commands feeding both the contented non-asker and the petitioner, covering those who come to the door and those whose need remains quiet.
terra: God sends water down in measure and makes it dwell in the earth; measured provision and the source section's س ك ن dwelling root are joined before any household fills a vessel from it.

luna: The section’s small household kindness is kept from a person in need; 24:22 tells people of means not to swear off giving to poor relatives and emigrants, but to pardon and continue giving, a specific case of reopening support after a grievance. | terra: People of means are forbidden to swear off giving relatives, the needy, and emigrants; it directly checks a well-supplied hand's decision to withhold.
terra: Household dependents seeking a contract for freedom are to receive some of the wealth God gave the householder, directing divinely supplied property toward the dependent's release.
terra: Household dependents and children below puberty must ask permission at three private times, giving a concrete interior scene for the section's small children and household members.
terra: When the children reach puberty they ask permission like adults, supplying the same maturity boundary that ends the section's definition of orphanhood.

luna: The section’s cited root glosses س ك ن as house and household and describes food that sustains a place; 24:61 names eating in one another’s homes and the homes of relatives and friends, a concrete Quranic scene of shared food across households. | terra: This ayah permits eating from one's own and relatives' houses, houses whose keys one holds, and friends' houses; it presents household stores as a shared network of access and trust.

luna: The section’s image turns on a hand so closed it refuses even a small, useful object; 25:67 sets the believers’ spending between extravagance and stinginess, giving a boundary for household giving rather than endorsing the closed hand. | terra: The servants' spending is neither wasteful nor stingy but balanced, clarifying that opening the household store does not mean destroying its ability to stand.
terra: Abraham identifies God as the one who feeds and gives drink, locating all filled dishes and cups under received provision rather than private ownership.
terra: Give full measure and do not be among those who cause loss; it answers the section's shaking-full vessel with an explicit obligation to fill honestly.
terra: Weigh with an even balance, completing the fair-measure scene rather than letting the vessel's appearance conceal a shortfall.
terra: Do not diminish people's things, broadening fair measure from grain to the useful possessions and benefits owed among people.
terra: Night is made so people may rest in it, a repeated repose sense that faintly clarifies why a dwelling and its sustaining goods share the section's root-family image.
terra: After helping strangers at the well, Moses withdraws to shade and tells God he is in need of whatever good is sent, voicing the needy asker's dependence without demanding from people.
terra: One woman then invites Moses to her household so her father can repay his help, moving the needy traveler from an open well toward shelter and recompense.
terra: Many creatures do not carry their own provision, yet God provides for them and for people; fear of an unstocked future is not proof that the hand must remain closed.
terra: Spouses are created so one may find سَكَن in the other, extending the section's dwelling root from the physical house to the repose that should characterize its relationships.

luna: This ayah repeats the provision-sharing comparison in 16:71 as a question about whether people would accept those under their authority as equal partners in their provision; it sharpens the section’s closed-hand image into a question of who is allowed a share.
terra: Give the relative, the needy, and the traveler their due, a repeated command that directs household means outward to recognizable claimants.
terra: Luqman tells his son that even a mustard-seed-sized deed hidden in rock will be brought forth by God, joining household instruction of a child with the visibility of the smallest act.
terra: The address to the Prophet's household joins remaining within the houses with establishing prayer and giving alms, bringing domestic space, worship, and material duty into one frame.

luna: The section develops the home as the place where a host prepares food for guests; 33:53 describes guests entering the Prophet’s home, eating when invited, and leaving afterward, giving a domestic boundary around hospitality. | terra: Rules for entering the Prophet's houses for a meal protect both hospitality and household privacy, setting a boundary around access to a home's prepared food.

terra: Solomon's workers make basin-like dishes and fixed cauldrons, directly supplying the Quranic counterpart to the section's bowls and pots, here enlarged into signs of abundant provision and grateful use.
terra: Whatever is spent, God replaces it; this gives theological force to the section's observation that releasing a useful object or provision need not diminish the home.
terra: No one can withhold mercy God opens or release what He withholds, setting divine control of supply against petty human control of a pot, bucket, or meal.

luna: The section’s ط ع م root links household food with feeding a person who asks; 36:47 stages the refusal itself: the deniers answer that they should feed someone God could feed, exposing the excuse behind withholding. | terra: When told to spend from God's provision, the unbelievers answer, أَنُطْعِمُ مَن لَّوْ يَشَآءُ ٱللَّهُ أَطْعَمَهُ; the stocked household turns divine provision into its excuse for not feeding.

luna: The section describes filling and serving from a vessel; 37:45 shows a cup of pure drink circulated among the people of Paradise, a specific scene of provision passed from hand to hand. | terra: A cup from a flowing spring is passed around among the blessed, making circulation rather than possession the action of the vessel.
terra: Solomon is told that God's gift may be bestowed or withheld without account; this exceptional divine authorization marks the opposite boundary from ordinary people's accountable withholding.
terra: God makes night for rest and day for sight, another repeated non-household use of the repose underlying the section's س ك ن associations.
terra: Those who do not give the purifying due are condemned, a broader legal instance of retaining a benefit that is owed beyond oneself.
terra: God apportions the earth's sustenance for those who ask, scaling the section's household provisions up to a measured world intended for claimants.
terra: If provision were expanded without limit people would transgress, so God sends it by measure; the ayah distinguishes measured supply from both deficient giving and destructive excess.
terra: Water is sent from heaven in due measure and revives dead land, a remote but concrete source for the water eventually carried in the section's loanable bucket.

luna: The section describes everyday bowls and useful household vessels and asks what it means to withhold them; 43:71 depicts trays of gold and cups circulated among the people of Paradise, a specific image of shared vessels and provision. | terra: Golden plates and cups are passed around in Paradise; the costly setting magnifies the ordinary social motion the section asks of cheap household ware.

luna: The section’s named root م ن ع makes withholding the central act; 47:38 contrasts the call to spend with whoever then withholds, and says that withholding harms the person who does it. | terra: Those called to spend who are stingy are stingy only against themselves, overturning the householder's belief that withholding preserves his household.
terra: مَنَّاعٍ لِّلْخَيْرِ again makes withholding good a defining charge, not an insignificant choice about a cheap object.
terra: فِى غَمْرَةٍ سَاهُونَ repeats the source section's س ه و wording in its Quranic sense of heedlessness, marking the lexical boundary across which the commentary also hears a porch or rack.

luna: The source section glosses م ع ن as small, easy household benefit and as recognized good; 51:19 says that in the righteous people’s wealth is a known right for the asker and deprived person, making even a small share a claim rather than mere favor. | terra: Their wealth contains a right for the asker and the deprived, so the arrival at the door discloses an existing claim rather than requesting an optional leftover.

luna: The section’s host gloss centers the people received in a household; 51:24 names Abraham’s honored guests, identifying the visitors whose meal and welcome continue in 51:26–27. | terra: Abraham's visitors are introduced as honored guests, establishing the household stance that his quiet preparation and presentation of food enact in 51:26-27.

luna: The source section’s cited dictionary gloss for طاعم and مطعام describes a host who receives guests generously; 51:26 shows Abraham going to his household and bringing a fat calf, the preparation that makes the meal in 51:27 possible. | terra: Abraham quietly goes to his household and returns with a fat calf, showing the interior store mobilized for guests rather than kept behind the door.

luna: The section describes a household host and vessels used to serve food; 51:27 shows Abraham placing the calf before his guests and inviting them to eat, a direct scene of open hospitality against the refused guest and asker. | terra: He places the food before the guests and invites them to eat, completing the movement from household provision to the visitor's reach.
terra: God seeks neither provision nor feeding from creatures, marking the limit of the provider analogy: humans feed the needy from what they themselves receive.
terra: God is the Provider and possessor of firm power, completing 51:57's statement that He seeks no provision or feeding and grounding human food in received supply.
terra: يُدَعُّونَ إِلَىٰ نَارِ جَهَنَّمَ دَعًّا uses the source section's د ع ع root for forceful shoving; the shover of the orphan is confronted with the same violence as punishment.

luna: The section’s household utensils are useful because they pass between people with food and drink; 52:23 depicts a cup passed among the people of Paradise, making circulation of a shared vessel explicit. | terra: People pass a cup among one another, making shared use of a vessel the scene's central action rather than private retention.
terra: أَعْطَىٰ قَلِيلًا وَأَكْدَىٰ describes one who gives a little and then stops, making the boundary of a tiny kindness itself morally revealing.

luna: The section develops filling and measuring a vessel; 55:8 says not to transgress in the balance, while 55:9 specifies not making it deficient, so this verse supplies the broader boundary around the next ayah’s measure.

luna: The section’s cited dictionary form دعدع مكيالا means shaking a measure to take its full contents; 55:9 commands establishing weight with justice and not making the balance deficient, directly bounding the measure image. | terra: Establish weight justly and do not make the balance deficient; the command gives the filled-vessel image its rule of exactness.
terra: Everlasting youths circulate among the blessed, supplying the act of passing that belongs to the cups and pitchers named in 56:18.

luna: The section names a shelf of useful household things and a bowl filled with food; 56:18 pictures cups, ewers, and a drink vessel circulated among the people of Paradise, a concrete scene of serving vessels in use. | terra: Cups, pitchers, and a filled drinking vessel are carried in Paradise; the object match with the section's shelf of containers is exact, though this ayah does not itself concern household generosity.
terra: People must spend from that over which God made them successors, reframing the objects and provisions inside the house as entrusted holdings.
terra: The promise to multiply a good loan to God reframes release from possession as recoverable gain, challenging anxiety over lending a small useful thing.
terra: Charitable men and women are described as lending God a good loan that is multiplied, joining actual giving to the section's ordinary logic of a borrowed item returned.

luna: The section explicitly names a miserly, withholding person through root م ن ع; 57:24 describes people who are stingy and urge others to stinginess, a direct parallel to the disposition in the image. | terra: Those who are stingy and command people to stinginess reproduce both failures in the section: the closed hand and the refusal to encourage provision for the needy.

luna: This ayah requires feeding sixty poor people when the prescribed fast cannot be performed; the measured number and meal make the section’s food for the miskin a specific act of provision. | terra: Feeding sixty needy people is required when the other forms of expiation cannot be performed, again making actual household provision the religious act.

luna: The ayah assigns communal wealth to relatives, orphans, the needy, and travelers so it will not circulate only among the rich; this directly counters the section’s image of useful provisions kept within one household. | terra: Public wealth is assigned to relatives, orphans, the needy, and travelers so that it does not circulate only among the rich, preventing stocked resources from remaining on one social shelf.
terra: The poor emigrants have been expelled from their homes and property; their loss of dwelling and goods supplies the concrete need answered by the household generosity of 59:9.

luna: The section’s hand withholds ordinary household benefits from a neighbor; 59:9 describes the Helpers welcoming newcomers and preferring them with their resources even when they themselves are needy, the household ethic’s opposite. | terra: The people of the home prefer arriving migrants over themselves despite their own need and are guarded from greed, reversing the stocked house that protects trivial goods from a neighbor.
terra: The hypocrites command others not to spend on those with the Messenger so they will disperse; deliberately closing provision becomes a means of driving needy people away.
terra: People are commanded to spend before death makes them beg for a delay in which to give charity, exposing how the supposedly postponable small good becomes irretrievable.
terra: Wealth and children are declared a test immediately before the commands to resist greed and spend, making the household's dependents and stores the very site of moral trial.
terra: Spending and being protected from the soul's greed describe success, naming the inward release required before the hand will take a useful thing down from the shelf.
terra: A good loan to God is multiplied and forgiven, supplying the promised return that the householder fails to trust when guarding trivial goods.
terra: Divorced women are not to be expelled from their houses during the waiting period, making continued dwelling itself part of the vulnerable household member's protection.
terra: House divorced women where you dwell according to your means, do not constrain them, and support pregnancy; shelter and provision are duties of the household holder.
terra: Each person must spend according to what God has given, and ease follows hardship; measured means define responsible provision without making scarcity an excuse to give nothing.
terra: Who could provide if God withheld His provision? The question reverses 36:47's excuse by making divine supply a reason for humility, not for refusing to feed.
terra: مَنَّاعٍ لِّلْخَيْرِ names the habitual withholder of good, joining the source dictionary's mennāʿ to its explanation of māʿūn as every recognized good.

luna: The section’s household scene has a person guarding useful things and food from someone who asks; the garden owners in 68:24 explicitly resolve that no poor person should enter to collect its fruit, a close parallel of planned exclusion from provision.

luna: The section shows goods kept back from a needy visitor; after the garden owners bar the poor in 68:24, 68:25 shows them setting out early with determined purpose to harvest, completing the deliberate withholding scene.

luna: The section’s cited wording ولا يحض على طعام المسكين is repeated in 69:34 as part of the account of the people of the left; this ayah makes the refusal to urge feeding the poor an explicit charge. | terra: وَلَا يَحُضُّ عَلَىٰ طَعَامِ ٱلْمِسْكِينِ repeats the section's failure to urge food for the needy and makes it part of the condemned person's own record.
terra: مَنُوعًا is the very withholding disposition named by the section's dictionary form; 70:22-25 oppose it with prayer and a recognized share for the deprived.

terra: Those who pray are named as the exception to the human being who becomes withholding when touched by good, providing the bridge from 70:21 to constant prayer and the needy person's known share.
terra: Constancy in prayer describes those exempted from the withholding impulse of 70:21, contrasting with prayer detached from the pantry's claims.

luna: The section depicts practical goods and food kept from people in need; 70:24 says a known right is set within the believers’ wealth, and 70:25 identifies the asker and deprived person, completing who holds that right. | terra: Their wealth contains a known right, turning what might look like a voluntary small favor into an assigned share.

luna: This ayah identifies the beneficiaries of the wealth right in 70:24 as the asker and deprived; it makes the section’s person coming to request a pot, water, or food recognizable as a claimant to provision. | terra: The known right belongs to the asker and the deprived, naming both the person at the door and the needy person who does not ask.
terra: The command to establish prayer and give alms is immediately followed by lending God a good loan, placing worship, due provision, and recoverable giving in one instruction.
terra: The people of Saqar confess that they were not among those who prayed; 74:44 immediately pairs that failure with not feeding the needy, matching the surah's prayer-and-pantry test.

luna: The source section centers food for the poor and the refusal to offer it; in 74:44 the people of the Fire name not feeding the poor among their own failures, giving the omission a stated consequence. | terra: وَلَمْ نَكُ نُطْعِمُ ٱلْمِسْكِينَ is the confessed omission of the act the section's stocked house could perform, paired with neglected prayer in 74:43.

luna: The section’s cited ط ع م root covers food, feeding, and hospitality, and it names the orphan and poor as those left without it; 76:8 depicts feeding the poor, orphan, and captive while the givers themselves love the food, turning withheld household provision into costly care. | terra: وَيُطْعِمُونَ ٱلطَّعَامَ names the act the house in the section withholds and places the needy and orphan together as its recipients.

luna: The section cites 76:8 as food given to the poor and orphan despite the givers’ love of it; 76:9 continues that same meal scene and says they feed for God’s sake without seeking repayment or thanks, clarifying the motive behind the provision. | terra: The feeders say they act for God's face and seek neither reward nor thanks, giving the inner stance opposite to display and possessive calculation over household goods.

luna: The section’s dish, pot, and other household utensils are shown empty or full according to how people share; 76:15 depicts silver vessels and glass cups being passed among the people of Paradise, a concrete Quranic scene of vessels in circulation. | terra: Silver vessels and cups are circulated among the righteous, a concrete positive image of containers moving between hands instead of remaining unused on a shelf.

luna: The section develops shaking a measure until the container is full; 76:16 describes clear cups of silver measured in precise proportion, completing the vessels in 76:15 with an explicit measure. | terra: The vessels are precisely measured, joining the section's container and full-measure images in the continuation of the surah that earlier praised feeding the needy and orphan.
luna: The section’s household containers are for food or drink; 76:17 continues the serving scene with a cup mixed with ginger, showing the vessels in 76:15–16 carrying a drink.
luna: This ayah names the spring from which the cup in 76:17 is mixed; it completes the provision scene attached to measured cups, though the spring itself is not a household object.
terra: The human being is told to look at his food, opening a sequence that traces what fills the household dish back through water, earth, and grain.
terra: God pours water abundantly, the first material contribution to the food whose source the eater is commanded to inspect.
terra: God splits the earth open, continuing the production chain that precedes any grain poured into a domestic measure.
terra: Grain is made to grow from the opened earth, directly supplying the substance the section pictures settling into a shaken measure.
terra: The crops are provision for people and their livestock, concluding that the entire food sequence is supplied benefit rather than self-created household property.

luna: The section’s measure is shaken until the full amount settles; 83:1 announces woe for the mutaffifin, and 83:2–3 specify their practice of taking full measure but giving less, reversing the filled measure. | terra: The warning to those who defraud in measure judges the same vessel the section imagines being filled; 83:2-3 specify the selfish asymmetry.

luna: The section’s image is a measure filled to capacity; 83:2 describes people who take full measure for themselves, and 83:3 supplies the corresponding short measure they give others, exposing the asymmetry. | terra: They demand a full measure when receiving from people, the acquisitive half of the household selfishness that keeps useful goods and food for itself.

luna: The source section’s cited dictionary form دعدع مكيالا is shaking a measure so it contains the full amount; 83:3 gives the opposite practice, shorting people when measuring or weighing, making the image’s filling and withholding a question of another person’s due. | terra: They cause loss when measuring or weighing for others, the exact contrary of shaking a measure until the recipient's vessel is full.
terra: Cups are set ready for use, a plausible visual counterpart to utensils taken down and made available; the surrounding scene is Paradise rather than a neighbor's house.

luna: The source section defines the orphan as a child whose father has died and describes him being pushed away; 89:17 names failure to honor the orphan, directly setting that treatment against the duty the scene violates. | terra: كَلَّا بَل لَّا تُكْرِمُونَ ٱلْيَتِيمَ directly condemns failure to honor the orphan; 89:18 adds the matching refusal to urge feeding.

luna: The section quotes the root ط ع م for food and feeding and says the man does not urge food for the poor; 89:18 likewise rebukes people for not urging one another to feed the poor, a close formulation of the image’s neglected encouragement. | terra: وَلَا تَحَٰٓضُّونَ عَلَىٰ طَعَامِ ٱلْمِسْكِينِ closely repeats 107:3 and follows failure toward the orphan, preserving the section's child-and-food sequence.
terra: After failure toward the orphan and needy, the passage charges people with devouring inheritance greedily; goods that should sustain the vulnerable are consumed into the powerful household.
terra: Intense love of wealth completes the explanation for 89:17-19: attachment to stored value produces both dishonoring the orphan and refusal to urge feeding.

luna: The section’s food image is household nourishment withheld from the needy; 90:14 names the act of feeding on a day of hunger, making the provision concrete rather than an abstract gift. Verses 90:15–16 specify the orphan and person in misery. | terra: Feeding on a day of severe hunger turns the section's filled dish into help precisely when food is hardest to release; 90:15-16 name its recipients.

luna: This ayah names an orphan who is a near relative as a recipient of the difficult ascent; 90:14 supplies the feeding scene, while this verse makes kinship and orphanhood part of who receives care. | terra: The hungry recipient is an orphan of near kin, bringing the fatherless child inside the circle of household relation rather than leaving the child at the door.

luna: This ayah names a poor person in misery as a recipient of the difficult ascent; 90:14 supplies the feeding action, and this verse specifies the vulnerable person who corresponds to the section’s poor at the door. | terra: The other hungry recipient is a needy person in destitution, completing the same orphan-needy pairing that structures the section.
terra: The one who gives and remains mindful begins the sequence leading toward ease, opposing the hand that withholds the section's easy little thing.
terra: God eases the giver toward ease; the repeated ease makes a moral counterpart to the source dictionary's description of maʿn as a slight, easy thing.

luna: The section identifies a withholding man as stingy and tight-fisted; 92:8 describes one who is stingy and thinks himself self-sufficient, giving a specific account of the attitude behind keeping small household benefits back. | terra: The person who is stingy and imagines himself self-sufficient embodies the house that treats its stored provision as private independence.

luna: After the stingy person of 92:8, this ayah says he denies the best; it adds the refusal that leads into the consequence in 92:10, matching the section’s act of withholding rather than merely its household setting.
terra: The miser is eased toward hardship, reversing his assumption that keeping the easy, little object makes life secure.

luna: The source section’s dictionary gloss for يَتِيم identifies the child whose father has died; 93:6 recalls God finding the Prophet an orphan and giving shelter (فَآوَى), a direct counterimage to pushing the fatherless child away. | terra: The reminder that God found the addressee an orphan and gave shelter makes a dwelling the answer to lost guardianship, directly completing the section's homeless child image.
terra: God found the addressee in need and made him sufficient, placing received provision between remembered orphanhood and the commands not to oppress the orphan or rebuff the asker.

luna: The section’s named word ٱلْيَتِيم is the orphan whom the man pushes; 93:9 gives the explicit boundary فَلَا تَقْهَرْ, not to oppress the orphan, reversing the act in the image. | terra: فَأَمَّا ٱلْيَتِيمَ فَلَا تَقْهَرْ forbids overpowering the orphan, a direct moral reversal of the hand that forcefully pushes the child away.
terra: وَأَمَّا ٱلسَّآئِلَ فَلَا تَنْهَرْ forbids rebuffing the person who asks, covering the neighbor who comes for food or a small household implement.
terra: Whoever does an atom's weight of good will see it, supporting the section's insistence that a trivial household favor remains a real act.
terra: Whoever does an atom's weight of evil will see it, completing 99:7's assurance that a tiny good matters and applying the same scale to withholding it.
terra: The immediately preceding surah says God fed Quraysh against hunger and secured them against fear; a community so provisioned is exposed when it will not feed the needy or release a small aid.
